title: Bank of America's bad news may not be what investors think
detail:
Bank of America's bad news may not be what investors think
Mwangi Enos, Robert Davey
Mon, October 19, 2026 at 1:17 PM CDT 5 min read
BAC
Trade BAC on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Just the other day, I covered Bank of America CEO Brian Moynihan addressing a $1.2 billion troubling problem for failing to report $5 billion in suspicious transactions.

You may be asking how a bank that size could let such a serious compliance issue slip through the cracks, especially when customers trust it to safeguard their money.

The $1.2 billion fine landed in a quarter when Bank of America (BAC) still brought in $30 billion in revenue, up 3% from a year ago but short of the $30.58 billion analysts expected. Reported earnings were $0.91 per share for the third quarter of fiscal 2026.

"We put lots of resources against this. Thousands of extra teammates," Moynihan said, adding that the bank lowered its reporting thresholds and the penalty went through last quarter. He said the bank is "deep into remediation activities,' as I highlighted previously.

However, investors want to know whether the fine and the fee miss are the last surprises.

Also Read: Bank of America sees another interest-rate surprise 

Bank of America's fine and fee miss rattle the stock

Morgan Stanley's answer is a cautious maybe. The firm kept an Overweight rating but cut its price target to $61 from $67, 18% above the $51.39 share price, in a report shared with TheStreet.

Morgan Stanley wrote that the OCC and FinCEN investigation fine and the fee miss added noise, but that the stock's drop suggests it is "closer to being de-risked."

Shares have slipped 5.36% this year through Oct. 16 on a total return basis, according to Yahoo Finance, and Morgan Stanley says they trade at 9.7 times 2027 earnings. It cut its target multiple to 11.5x from 12.25x. It also trimmed 2027 EPS by 3% to $5.28 and 2026 EPS by 1% to $4.59 on lower fee income.

More Bank of America:

BofA sets massive $10 billion Ciena backlog target

A bond market revolt pushes a key rate to 19-year high

Bank of America stock slides after CEO's troubling message

According to its Q3 fiscal 2026 report, Adjusted earnings of $1.08 a share missed consensus by about 1%, primarily due to weaker trading. Fixed income revenue fell 17% as clients pulled back after a sharp move in interest rates, particularly in credit, mortgages and municipal bonds. Equities still delivered a record third quarter, with revenue up 10%.

The miss was not a surprise to everyone. Management had warned in September that the quarter would be softer, and it does not expect as much of the usual fourth-quarter seasonal slowdown.

On the fine, management said the technology and people needed for remediation are already funded and in the expense run rate. It confirmed no asset cap is in place, meaning regulators have not limited the bank's growth, and said the work will not crowd out investment elsewhere.

title: Should You Buy Bank of America Stock After a $1.2 Billion Regulatory Fine?
detail:
Should You Buy Bank of America Stock After a $1.2 Billion Regulatory Fine?
Bram Berkowitz, The Motley Fool
Mon, October 19, 2026 at 7:20 AM CDT 5 min read
BAC
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Following its third-quarter earnings report, Bank of America's (NYSE: BAC) stock fell 4.7% on Oct. 14 in its worst performance in 18 months. At one point, the stock fell almost 9%, a huge move for a stock like Bank of America.

Not only did the bank report weak results, it also disclosed a $1.2 billion regulatory fine for money-laundering violations. Should investors buy the stock after the poor earnings results and regulatory fine?

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: The Motley Fool.
A disappointing quarter

Bank of America reported $0.91 per share in profit on revenue of $30.12 billion. Both numbers came up short of Wall Street's expectations, but excluding the $1.2 billion fine, the bank would have reported $1.08 in earnings per share, missing estimates by only $0.02.

Still, there was certainly weakness in parts of the bank's business. CEO Brian Moynihan had previously warned of a soft quarter in investment banking and trading, and that warning ultimately played out.

Investment banking fees fell nearly 16% year over year in Q3, while total sales and trading revenue fell over $2 billion from the prior quarter and was also down nearly 5.5% year over year.

On the bright side, net interest income (NII), the spread revenue banks make between the interest they pay on interest-bearing deposits such as liabilities and what they earn on interest-earning assets such as loans, increased $1.2 billion year over year to $16.6 billion in Q3.

NII is a key revenue source for most banks. On the company's earnings call, CFO Alastair Borthwick told analysts that NII should grow about 8% year over year in 2026, hitting the top end of management's guidance, which had been revised higher on multiple occasions earlier this year.

Borthwick also said the bank expects NII to grow at least 8% in 2027, assuming three quarter-point interest rate hikes between now and June 2027. Additionally, credit quality remained benign and showed no alarming deterioration during the quarter.

Anti-money-laundering fine

As mentioned, banking regulators fined Bank of America $1.2 billion in total, alleging that the money-center bank failed to report over $5 billion in suspicious transactions over several years, including those involving national security risks.

Moynihan addressed the issue on the live conference call with analysts, saying the bank has been aware of the issues and has already allocated funds and resources for remediation within its expense base.

title: JPMorgan Slashes Q3 Share Buybacks: Is Organic Growth a Better Bet?
detail:
JPMorgan Slashes Q3 Share Buybacks: Is Organic Growth a Better Bet?
Zacks Equity Research
Mon, October 19, 2026 at 8:00 AM CDT 2 min read
JPM
BAC
C
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

JPMorgan JPM has sharply reduced its share repurchases, signaling a strategic shift toward reinvesting capital in its businesses. The banking giant reported net share buybacks of just $664 million in the third quarter of 2026, down nearly 89% from $6.2 billion in the preceding quarter.

CEO Jamie Dimon emphasized that investing in JPMorgan's franchise and supporting clients remain higher priorities than repurchasing shares. With approximately $30 billion in excess capital, the bank sees opportunities to deploy funds into businesses capable of generating attractive long-term returns.

The strategy appears promising, given JPMorgan's diversified operations and strong market position. Investments in technology, branch expansion, commercial banking, wealth management and international operations could strengthen customer relationships and support sustainable revenue growth. Rising demand for financing across infrastructure and other capital-intensive sectors presents additional opportunities for business expansion.

JPMorgan's financial strength provides considerable flexibility. The bank ended the third quarter with $304 billion in Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital and a standardized CET1 ratio of 13.9%. Its profitability also remained robust, with a return on tangible common equity of 20%.

However, fewer buybacks may limit near-term earnings growth, while the higher 2026 adjusted expense outlook of $108.6 billion underscores cost pressures. Returns on investments may also take time to materialize. Nevertheless, JPMorgan's capital allocation strategy appears prudent. Prioritizing high-return growth opportunities over repurchases at elevated valuations could strengthen its competitive position and create greater long-term shareholder value.

Citigroup and Bank of America in Terms of Q3 Share Buybacks

Citigroup C repurchased approximately $3 billion of shares in the third quarter of 2026, bringing year-to-date buybacks to $13.3 billion. As of Sept. 30, 2026, $23 billion worth of shares remained available under the share repurchase program. 

Citigroup returned $4.1 billion to shareholders, including dividends, reflecting its continued focus on capital distributions alongside investments in business growth and improving profitability.

Bank of America BAC repurchased $6 billion worth of shares during third-quarter 2026, reflecting its commitment to shareholder returns. As of Sept. 30, 2026, almost $11 billion remained under its $40 billion share repurchase authorization. 

Including $2.2 billion in dividends, Bank of America returned $8.3 billion to shareholders. The buybacks highlight management's confidence in its capital position, supported by a solid CET1 ratio of 10.9%.

title: US banks limit AI agents’ access to customer accounts – report
detail:
US banks limit AI agents’ access to customer accounts – report
Vidhya Edwards Munnangi
Mon, October 19, 2026 at 6:32 AM CDT 2 min read
C
BAC
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Citigroup and Bank of America are restricting AI agents from accessing customer accounts, joining JPMorgan Chase and Charles Schwab in tightening controls over automated financial tools, reported the Financial Times.

Banks fear agents will drain deposits by shifting idle cash to higher returns, the report noted.

Citi does not permit "third-party AI agents or assistants to log into a customer's account or transact directly within our digital banking platforms".

The restriction was intended to protect customer accounts and information.

Bank of America is limiting AI agents' access to consumer deposits, according to a person familiar with the matter.

Chief executive Brian Moynihan said the bank was developing protocols to determine which party would be liable for payments authorised by AI.

"We strongly believe there should be a human in the loop to authorise money moving out of your account," Moynihan told CNBC.

According to sources, Wall Street executives have contacted Federal Reserve regulators about the growing use of AI agents for financial transactions.

Regulators have privately supported banks' decisions to block AI agents from client accounts, the news publication added.

Officials believe the law may need to clarify how customers authorise autonomous technology to act on their behalf, and who is liable if a transaction fails or causes a loss.

JPMorgan Chase chief executive Jamie Dimon said this week that the bank would limit AI agents' access to client accounts "because you don't want rogue agents and there could be thousands of them".

"We have to make sure we protect our customers in the right way. So, we're building tools to do that, too," Dimon said on the bank's third-quarter results call.

Charles Schwab chief executive Rick Wurster told Bloomberg that the brokerage, wealth-management, and banking company was blocking unauthorised AI agents attempting to transfer clients' money, including Meta Platforms' Muse.

For the first time in well over half a century, Berkshire Hathaway (NYSE:BRKA)(NYSE:BRKB) entered the year in uncharted territory. On Dec. 31, Warren Buffett retired as CEO, paving the way for his protégé, Greg Abel, to oversee the company's day-to-day operations and its closely watched $363 billion investment portfolio.

Abel didn't waste much time making his mark. He disposed of 16 stocks in the first quarter and pared down six others, including one of the Oracle of Omaha's core holdings, Bank of America (NYSE:BAC)(also known as BofA).

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Warren Buffett has officially passed the baton to Greg Abel. Image source: Getty Images.

In the six quarters leading up to Buffett's retirement, he was a persistent seller of BofA stock. This pattern has continued through Abel's first two quarters as CEO, with Buffett and Abel collectively selling more than 549 million shares since July 2024, or 53% of what had been a 1.03-billion-share position.

The writing looked to be on the wall that Bank of America would get the heave-ho -- but that may not be the case any longer.

Buffett and Abel collectively sold over 549 million shares of Bank of America

As recently as a few months ago, there were three reasons to believe that BofA's time as a prominent Berkshire Hathaway holding would come to an end.

Firstly, Buffett and Abel have always been sticklers for value. When the Oracle of Omaha first invested in BofA's preferred stock in August 2011, its common stock was trading at a 62% discount to book value. As recently as August, BofA peaked at a 65% premium to book value.

Secondly, Bank of America is the most interest-sensitive of the country's money-center banks. With the Federal Reserve lowering rates six times between September 2024 and December 2025, no large bank was at greater risk of its net interest income shrinking than BofA.

Third and finally, Greg Abel's first annual letter to shareholders excluded Bank of America in his discussion of companies that can compound over multiple decades.

The writing looked to be on the wall that Bank of America would soon get the heave-ho.

Image source: Getty Images.

Greg Abel's tune on Bank of America may have changed

While additional selling is possible, several catalysts that had made Bank of America stock less attractive have reversed course.

title: Bank of America CEO addresses a troubling banking problem
detail:
Bank of America CEO addresses a troubling banking problem
Mwangi Enos, Celine Provini
Sat, October 17, 2026 at 4:03 PM CDT 5 min read
BAC
Trade BAC on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

A few years ago, I remember helping my elderly neighbor set up a new bank account after her branch closed. The process involved more paperwork than buying a car — identity verification, source-of-funds questions, and transaction-monitoring disclosures. 

She found it exhausting. I found it excessive. I remember the banker saying the requirements had gotten stricter "because of what happened with the big banks."

I thought about that incident when the Treasury Department announced more than $1.21 billion in penalties against Bank of America for allegedly doing the opposite.

According to the U.S. Treasury press release, the bank failed to report more than $5 billion in suspicious transactions over several years. Some of that activity was linked to Chinese money laundering networks and operations along the southwest border.

You will most certainly be scrutinized for opening a checking account. The U.S. second-largest bank, meanwhile, was not flagging billions in activity that regulators say included narcotics trafficking proceeds and potential trade-based money laundering.

BAC is down 4.49% year-to-date, according to Yahoo Finance, after falling 2% in after-hours trading on the penalty announcement Oct. 13, the day before CEO Brian Moynihan was scheduled to report Q3 earnings.

Also Read: Bank of America sees another interest-rate surprise

Here is what the Treasury actually found, and why regulators escalated

The $1.2 billion penalty is the third-largest in Treasury history, according to the Treasury announcement. The $750 million civil money penalty from the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) is the largest the OCC has ever levied against any bank.

The core finding? Bank of America signed a cease-and-desist order with regulators in 2024 to fix its anti-money-laundering program. Regulators said the problems continued after that order. 

Treasury said the bank "prioritized its revenues" while minimizing compliance resources, and relied so heavily on law enforcement referrals from other institutions that it effectively outsourced part of its own responsibility for detecting suspicious activity.

title: Bank of America: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors
detail:
Bank of America: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors
The Motley Fool Team, The Motley Fool
Sat, October 17, 2026 at 1:28 PM CDT 3 min read
BAC
Trade BAC on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Oct. 14, 2026, Bank of America (NYSE:BAC) announced adjusted net income of $8.1 billion. A $1.2 billion regulatory settlement charge reduced reported net income to $6.9 billion. Rising loan yields continue driving core earnings higher. Three things management said stand out.

1. Net Interest Income Growth Will Exceed 8% in 2027

Net interest income, or NII -- the difference between what a bank earns on loans and pays on deposits -- is accelerating as fixed-rate assets reprice into higher yields. Management raised its guidance above original targets.

For 2027, we currently expect full-year growth of NII to be 8% or more, higher than 2026, and again, higher than our original 5%-7% range.
-- Alastair Borthwick, Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer

2. Regulatory Settlement Costs Are Already Baked Into Expenses

A $1.2 billion non-tax-deductible regulatory settlement charge for failure to adhere to anti-money laundering compliance lowered reported earnings. Management already built the ongoing technology and staffing costs directly into its standard operating expense base.

Third, we have committed the resources, and the ongoing cost remediation is embedded in our company's expense base.
-- Brian Moynihan, Chair and Chief Executive Officer

3. Low Loan-to-Deposit Ratios Protect Margins From Price Wars

Total deposits reached $2 trillion, funding $1.25 trillion in loans. Because the bank holds substantial excess liquidity, it doesn't need to offer high interest rates to retain customer deposits.

Our focus on operating deposits and our low loan-to-deposit ratio allow us to compete on capabilities rather than price.
-- Alastair Borthwick, Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer

Looking Ahead

Commercial borrowing and account growth show no signs of slowing down. Management expects operating leverage -- growing revenue faster than operating expenses -- to resume in the fourth quarter. Fixed-rate loans continue repricing into higher yields, while artificial intelligence tools trim routine technology costs.

What our clients are actually doing is continuing to point to a resilient and growing economy in the U.S.
-- Brian Moynihan, Chair and Chief Executive Officer

Core organic growth in consumer checking accounts and commercial relationships provides a durable moat against market volatility. Broad business diversity insulates total earnings when investment banking and trading activity cool down.

Our balance sheet and capital remain strong, and we continue to invest in technology and develop AI capabilities to support long-term growth. This quarter demonstrates the strength of our franchise and the value of our diversified business model.
-- Brian Moynihan, Chair and Chief Executive Officer
